title: Dēpology Design System
subtitle: Turning mobile commerce friction into reusable navigation, buybox, cart, checkout, and responsive product-page patterns.
problem: Depology, a rapidly growing Korean skincare brand with a strong Instagram presence in the US market, was preparing to launch multiple new products for shadow testing through paid advertising. They needed optimized product landing pages to maximize conversion rates in their ad-to-web customer journey. However, initial analysis revealed critical friction points: heatmap data showed users struggling with the mobile product buybox, while analytics indicated high drop-off rates and shortened session lengths tied to confusing header navigation on mobile devices. These UX issues were directly hindering conversion potential at a crucial growth moment.
solution: A data-driven redesign focused on the two highest-impact friction points: the mobile buybox and header navigation. After conducting thorough analysis of heatmaps, conversion funnels, and session behavior, new designs were proposed and validated through A/B testing. The redesigned mobile buybox streamlined the purchase flow with clearer CTAs and improved information hierarchy, while the simplified header navigation reduced cognitive load and improved discoverability. Following successful test runs and stakeholder presentations that secured buy-in from both product and marketing leadership, the changes were implemented across new product landing pages and ultimately adopted site-wide.
body: Depology was at an inflection point. The Korean skincare brand had built a devoted following on Instagram and was ready to scale through aggressive product launches and paid advertising. But there was a problem: their existing product pages weren't converting at the rates needed to justify increased ad spend. With multiple new products queued for shadow testing—a strategy where products are launched quietly to gauge market response before full rollout—the team needed landing pages that could turn Instagram traffic into customers efficiently.

The first step was diagnosis. Heatmap analysis revealed that mobile users were tapping repeatedly on elements within the product buybox, suggesting confusion about how to add items to cart or select variants. Conversion funnel data confirmed the suspicion: a significant percentage of users were abandoning their sessions at the product page stage. Session length metrics told another story—users who did engage were spending less time on site than expected, often bouncing after encountering the cluttered header navigation. These weren't assumptions; they were patterns backed by behavioral data.

Armed with these insights, the redesign focused on surgical improvements rather than wholesale changes. The mobile buybox was reimagined with a clearer visual hierarchy: variant selectors were made more prominent, the add-to-cart button was enlarged and repositioned for thumb-friendly access, and product information was reorganized to answer questions in the order customers naturally asked them. The header navigation was simplified dramatically, reducing menu options and improving the information architecture to help users find what they needed without overwhelming them. Every decision was testable, measurable, and directly tied to observed user behavior.

The validation process was methodical. Test runs were launched on select product pages, with conversion rates monitored daily. The results were striking: the new designs drove a conversion rate increase that validated every hypothesis. With data in hand, the pitch to product and marketing leadership was straightforward—these changes weren't subjective design preferences, they were proven performance improvements. The stakeholders backed the rollout, and the new UI was implemented first across all new product landing pages, then gradually adopted across the entire site. Depology's mobile experience had transformed from a conversion bottleneck into a growth engine.

title: Explainable Property Search
subtitle: A search prototype that shows renters how their messy query was understood before asking them to trust the results.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'can property search understand natural language?' to 'how does a renter know the system understood the messy parts of their request?' A query like 'studio near UCL under 2500, bills included, lift, quiet, not basement' carries budget, location, exclusions, amenities, and soft preferences in one sentence. Standard filters make the renter split that sentence apart and remember the rest while scanning listings.
solution: I kept the familiar search and filter model, then added a visible interpretation layer. The prototype turns the query into editable chips, separates hard exclusions from softer preferences, ranks structured JSON listings through a Python parser and scorer, and explains each match in plain language so users can correct the system before trusting it.

title: Worldschooling
subtitle: A launchable education-travel platform that replaced a heavy booking build with programme comparison, eligibility, and deposit flow.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'how do we build the full education-travel platform?' to 'which decisions must a parent make before paying a deposit?' The planned first release included campus pages, subject pages, programme pages, booking, blog, and search. That scope would have delayed launch, while parents and students still mainly needed to compare programme tiers, understand eligibility, and know what commitment the deposit represented.
solution: I reduced the first-release journey to the decisions that mattered: programme discovery, tier comparison, detail pages, eligibility form, and a universal deposit payment link. The tradeoff was less automation than a custom booking engine, but it kept comparison and commitment clear while removing months of portal development. Homepage categories and recommendation cards were used to expose mid-tier and premium programmes without forcing a hard upsell.
body: The diagnosis moved from 'which pages should the startup launch with?' to 'which decisions must a parent make before paying a deposit?' The original architecture was large enough to freeze the team in planning: campus pages, subject pages, programme pages, booking, blog, and search. I mapped the first release around the smaller set of decisions that actually had to happen before commitment: compare programmes, check fit, submit eligibility details, and pay a deposit.

I replaced the custom booking portal with a simpler path: homepage, programme filter, detail page, eligibility form, and universal deposit link. This was less automated than a full booking engine, but it let the business launch without hiding the important steps. Parents could still understand what was included, students could still compare options, and the team could still collect the information needed before confirming a place.

The programme hierarchy became the main design lever. The homepage category selector gave mid-tier programmes a visible entry point, while entry-level detail pages included recommendation cards for related higher-value options. The aim was not to push users harder. It was to make the next programme level visible at the moment when someone was already comparing dates, themes, and value.

The strongest outcome was launch readiness. In stakeholder review, the flow gave the founder a sales surface that could support conversations, fundraising, and early customer enquiries without waiting for a full booking system. The next proof point would be live funnel data: which categories people open, where parents leave the eligibility form, and which programme recommendations actually lead to deposit clicks.

title: Worldover.io
subtitle: A compliance prototype that separates risk, production, alerts, reporting, and evidence so operators can clear threshold cases with less context switching.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'how do we show more compliance data?' to 'what must an operator know before they can clear a threshold breach?' The earlier dashboard made risk status, production contribution, alert rules, report blockers, and evidence records compete on one surface, so users had to hold too much context in their head before deciding the next action.
solution: I kept the multi-tab model because the work changes by tab. Risk Command is where the operator decides the next action. Production explains contribution. Alerts manage escalation rules. Reporting shows what blocks a draft. Evidence proves whether the record can survive review. The dummy data model makes entity selection change severity, readiness, facts, blockers, and evidence rather than acting as a label-only filter.

content.value: The diagnosis moved from 'how do we show more compliance data?' to 'what must an operator know before they can clear a threshold breach?' A single annual threshold case can involve production plans, legal entity scope, registration limits, stale data, plant owners, evidence imports, and report-generation blockers. The old dashboard made those jobs compete for attention on one surface.

content.title: Why the live demo looks different from the original delivery
content.value: The embedded Risk Command Centre is a recent April 2026 update of the earlier Worldover delivery. The original work established the compliance dashboard direction and visual system. This newer demo returns to the same product problem and asks a narrower question: once a threshold risk is detected, what does the operator need to check, assign, or unblock before the case can move forward? That is why the live demo intentionally looks and behaves differently from the older dashboard screens.

content.title: Risk Command Centre
content.description: Change the entity selector to see the backend display conditions switch across the whole interface: case status, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and readiness all update from the dummy data model.

content.kicker: What improved from the old delivery
content.title: Five design upgrades in the April 2026 demo

items.title: From passive dashboard to action command centre
items.value: The older delivery focused on surfacing compliance data. The updated demo turns the same risk context into a workflow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, assign the next owner, and watch readiness change.

items.title: Clearer mindspace separation
items.value: Risk Command, Production, Alerts, Reporting, and Evidence now live in separate tabs. Each tab has one job, so operators do not have to compare tables, charts, rules, and audit records at the same time.

items.title: Entity-aware data behavior
items.value: The prototype is backed by structured dummy data with entity-specific display conditions. Switching from group view to Germany, France, or UK changes severity, metrics, readiness, production facts, alerts, reporting blockers, evidence, and the resolution drawer.

items.title: Clearer compliance reasoning
items.value: The case now shows what is above threshold, what blocks closure, who owns the next action, and which evidence is still missing before reporting can proceed.

items.title: Cleaner interaction states
items.value: The April 2026 demo applies a tighter Worldover-inspired visual language, clearer text hierarchy, resolved z-index/layout issues, accessible threshold labels, and browser-tested responsive behaviour.

content.value: The main UX decision was to keep multiple tabs rather than collapse everything into one large dashboard. Risk Command is for deciding what to do. Production is for factory contribution and threshold consumption. Alerts are for rules and escalation. Reporting is for blockers and draft gates. Evidence is for imports and audit trail. That separation makes the interface calmer because each tab has one job.

Inside Risk Command, the flow is intentionally narrow: detect the signal, decide the mitigation, then assign the work. The UI still exposes supporting data, but it does not ask the operator to interpret every table before taking the next step.

content.caption: The April 2026 update separates risk, production, alerts, reporting, and evidence into distinct work modes.

content.value: To make the prototype realistic, I mapped a dummy backend payload that covers the display states the interface needs: severity classes, readiness rules, chemical records, entity views, production charts, alert rules, reporting sections, evidence records, drawer actions, and empty states. Entity selection is no longer a label-only filter; it changes the full display context.

title: Travel to Qin
subtitle: A trust-building travel site for international visitors comparing China itineraries after the 2024 visa policy change.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'the site needs to look more premium' to 'what does a foreign visitor need to believe before asking about a China itinerary?' The old Shopify page could take a transaction, but it did not answer the questions that arrive before payment: who runs the trip, what the itinerary feels like, how support works, and why the agency is credible.
solution: I rebuilt the experience around proof before purchase: a video-led opening, itinerary sections, destination cards, service explanations, and a CMS structure the team could update without redesigning the page. The tradeoff was to prioritise trust and content clarity before deeper booking automation, because the first problem was not checkout. It was helping visitors feel ready to enquire.
body: The diagnosis moved from 'the site needs to look more premium' to 'what does a foreign visitor need to believe before asking about a China itinerary?' After the September 2024 visa policy change, Travel to Qin had a clearer market opening, but the old Shopify page was still built like a checkout. It did not explain the itinerary, the support model, the cultural experience, or why a visitor should trust the agency before making contact.

The first design decision was to put proof before purchase. I used brand cues from Chinese calligraphy and landscape painting, but kept the system practical: a clearer logo, a restrained travel palette, reusable content sections, and visual hierarchy that could carry both cultural imagery and service information. The goal was not decoration. It was to make the company feel legible to visitors arriving from social or search.

The landing page was structured around the questions a traveller asks before enquiring: what will I see, who guides the trip, how is the itinerary organised, and what makes the service credible? Video and imagery created the first impression, but the important work was the section order: destination context, itinerary detail, service explanation, and enquiry path. Moving from Shopify to a CMS gave the team a way to update trips and stories without rebuilding the page.

The strongest outcome was a more useful sales surface for stakeholder review and future campaigns. The site could now support social traffic, brochures, and app extension with the same visual language. The next proof point would be live enquiry data: which itinerary sections hold attention, which social channels produce qualified enquiries, and where visitors still need reassurance before contact.

images.caption: The redesign moved the site from transaction-first checkout to a trust-building travel surface with context, itinerary detail, and enquiry path.
Tour pages put itinerary proof before transaction: destination context, trip structure, support cues, and next-step clarity.
The same visual system could extend into mobile app and brochure surfaces without changing the core trust-building story.

title: Nihao Serica
subtitle: A 0-to-1 website and identity system shaped around first-visit trust, service clarity, and enquiry flow.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'how do we make the brand look finished?' to 'what does a first-time visitor need to understand before they trust Nihao Serica enough to enquire?' The work needed to make the offer, identity, proof points, and next step clear without relying on a long sales conversation.
solution: I shaped the first-release digital presence around the visitor's trust path: what the organisation does, why it is credible, what the user can do next, and how the brand should feel across the site. Because the current portfolio only has limited public evidence, the case is deliberately written as a concise delivery note rather than an inflated outcome story.

title: TUTU FUTURE
subtitle: A flexible study-tour identity system for programme categories that had outgrown the original hiking-focused brand.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'the logo looks dated' to 'the brand only explains one kind of programme.' TUTU FUTURE's original green hiking identity worked for outdoor trips, but it did not help students understand art, STEM, language, or city-culture programmes. The team needed one system that could flex across categories without creating a different mini-brand for every trip.
solution: I rebuilt the identity around repeatable programme categories. Colour, mascot use, layout templates, and bilingual lockups gave each programme type its own signal while keeping the materials recognisably TUTU FUTURE. The practical goal was asset production: posters, social posts, brochures, and student-facing communications that the team could adapt without redesigning from scratch.
body: The diagnosis moved from 'the logo looks dated' to 'the brand only explains one kind of programme.' The old green hiking identity worked for outdoor trips, but it did not help a student understand art, STEM, language, or city-culture programmes. The brand problem was not just taste. It was category clarity.

I kept the idea of exploration, but moved it away from literal hiking cues. The logo, typography, and bilingual lockup had to work on posters, social posts, brochures, and student-facing materials. The tradeoff was to keep the system simple enough for repeated production instead of designing a bespoke look for every programme.

Colour became the main navigation device. Language, art, STEM, outdoor, and culture programmes could each carry a different palette while sharing the same layout logic and mascot behaviour. That gave the team variation without fragmenting the brand.

The strongest outcome was an asset system the team could keep using. Campaign materials could change by programme type while still looking like one organisation. The next proof point would be usage data from real campaigns: which programme visuals get saved, shared, or lead to enquiry.

Programme colours give each category a clear signal while keeping the layouts and brand structure consistent.
Templates were designed for repeated production across posters, social posts, brochures, and student-facing communications.

title: Stair Aid
subtitle: A stair-specific crutch concept that lets users change length quickly when flat-ground walking turns into stair gait.
problem: The diagnosis moved from 'crutches are slow on stairs' to 'stair gait asks for a different crutch length than flat-ground walking.' Standard crutches are symmetrical on level ground, but stairs work better with a front-back stance. Manual adjustment takes too long and needs both hands, so users either climb with the wrong length or stop mid-staircase to change it.
solution: StairAid uses a one-handed trigger mechanism so each crutch can change length in about 3 seconds. The design keeps the adjustment fast, moves the locking mechanism inside the tube after prototype feedback, and uses a curved tip and forearm brace to support stair-specific movement.
body: The challenge began with a simple observation: stair gait asks for a different crutch length than flat-ground walking. On level surfaces, crutches are positioned symmetrically. On stairs, a diagonal stance with one crutch higher and one lower creates a more useful support triangle with the uninjured leg. Traditional crutches can do this only through slow manual adjustment.

I tested the idea with standard crutches first. Uneven crutch lengths reduced stair descent time from 8 seconds to 6 seconds and felt more stable in stair tests. That changed the design objective: the product did not need to reinvent the entire crutch. It needed a length adjustment mechanism that worked in seconds.

The technical solution evolved through multiple iterations. Early prototypes used an external locking system mounted around the crutch tube, but user feedback revealed aesthetic concerns and mechanical complexity. The second iteration moved the mechanism inside the tube, making it invisible from the outside while reducing part count and improving durability. The locking system uses a lever for linear motion input, a bike cable for motion transfer, and a wedge mechanism to convert vertical hand motion into horizontal locking force. An extension spring keeps the length locked by default, requiring only a trigger pull to release.

Three details carried the stair-specific design: the trigger release, the curved tip, and the forearm brace. The curved tip gives a concave surface for applying force during adjustment and a more secure contact point when the crutch is tilted on stairs. Nylon-66 30-GF was chosen for structural parts so the concept could stay lightweight while handling real-world loads.

images.caption: The problem framing moved from general crutch discomfort to the specific mismatch between flat-ground crutch length and stair gait.

The core innovation relies on uneven crutch lengths, enabling users to adopt a stable front-back stance on stairs. This specific gait ensures 3/4 of the body weight is supported, preventing recurrent injury.
The trigger lets users change crutch length in about 3 seconds per piece when moving between level ground and stairs.
The internal locking mechanism utilizes a lever, bike cable, and wedge system to translate vertical hand motion into a horizontal locking pin action, providing secure and rapid length adjustment.
